facts.statement: Role permissions are now stored per role as a list. The Role object returned by the roles API drops the 11 boolean fields (ShowConfiguration, ExecuteActions, AlterActions, AlterInvestigations, ShowAuditLogs, ShowSearch, ShowThreat, ShowHome, CreateThreat, ShowSubscription, ShowServiceAccounts) and has a Permissions array of numeric permission values plus an IsBuiltIn boolean.

Numeric role permission values: FullControl=0, ShowConfiguration=1, ExecuteActions=2, AlterActions=3, AlterInvestigations=4, ShowAuditLogs=5, ShowSearch=6, ShowThreat=7, CreateThreat=8, ShowHome=9, ShowSubscription=10, ShowServiceAccounts=11, ManageNtp=12, ViewAllInvestigations=13.
New role permission ManageNtp (12) controls who can manage the Netwrix Threat Prevention (NTP) gRPC integration configuration and trigger NTP actions. Every NTP management endpoint requires it.
facts.outOfScope: Writer decision: the NTP integration is a beta UI not meant for release, so it is left out of the 3.4 docs

facts.statement: New role permission ViewAllInvestigations (13) gives unrestricted visibility into every saved investigation (alert query), bypassing ownership, the public flag, and explicit access grants.

Access to investigations is now decided by permission, not role name. A user with ViewAllInvestigations sees all investigations. A user without ShowSearch is not given access through role-based sharing. Previously the Administrators and Report Administrator roles were matched by name and the Report Reviewer role was excluded by name.

On upgrade, the built-in Administrators role receives ManageNtp and ViewAllInvestigations, and the built-in Report Administrator role receives ViewAllInvestigations. Existing roles keep their current permissions.

Built-in roles (those that exist before upgrade, such as Administrators and Report Administrator) are marked IsBuiltIn. Updating or deleting a built-in role fails with "Role '<name>' is built-in and cannot be updated." or "Role '<name>' is built-in and cannot be deleted."

The FullControl permission passes every permission check. It is granted to the built-in Administrators role and to the built-in 'admin' account. It replaces the earlier match on the Administrators role name.
Role tables role_permission and role_permission_join replace the boolean permission columns on the role table. The migration copies existing flags into join rows and drops the columns.

New endpoint GET api/v1/Apptoken/{id}/token returns the raw value of an app token as { token }. It requires ShowConfiguration, returns 404 when the id is unknown, and writes an audit entry that records only the token id and name.
The audit log message for viewing a token reads: Application token '<name>' value viewed or copied.
Policy list responses no longer include the app token value. The AppToken.Token field returns "[REDACTED]". Use GET api/v1/Apptoken/{id}/token to read it.

New endpoint GET api/v1/Apptoken/BrokenTokens returns the names of app tokens that are no longer signed with the current signing key. It requires ShowConfiguration. The Apptoken object has a new Broken boolean.

A background check marks app tokens as broken or resolved and writes audit entries: "App token '<name>' is no longer signed with the current signing key." and "App token '<name>' issue has been resolved."
Creating an app token accepts only the Application and Agent types. Any other type returns 400 with "Only Application and Agent tokens can be created." The created token takes the type you send.

App token types now include Agent (3), alongside Application and Integration (2). On upgrade, tokens linked to an Integration service are retyped to Integration, and a new apptoken.broken column defaults to false. Agent tokens are not detected automatically.

When a honey token policy is read or its script is fetched and its app token is broken or deleted, Threat Manager creates a new app token and records the history entry "App token replaced. Honey Tokens must be re-deployed." The old token stays active until you delete it.

A remote Integration Service registration response (POST to the integration service registration endpoint) now returns RegisterIntegrationServiceResponse with an EncryptedStatusJwt instead of an empty 200.

New endpoint GET api/v1/ServiceStatus lets a remote service check that Threat Manager can reach it and that it accepts its token. It uses the status token issued at registration and returns 400 "The token does not name a machine." or "The token does not name a service type.", or 404 when no matching service exists. It is not audited.

Exporting logs on a Threat Manager install whose PostgreSQL database is on a different server no longer fails with 500. The export zip contains DatabaseLogs_PathNotFound.txt when the database log path does not exist on the local machine, or DatabaseLogs_NoFilesFound.txt when it exists but has no log files.
The log export endpoint now catches unexpected errors and returns 500 with "Failed to export logs. See server logs for details." The export file is named Logs_<version>_<yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss>.zip.

POST v1/Tag/TagObjects accepts a uniqueName with each object in ObjectTags ({ objectId, uniqueName }). The tagging response action and the object details UI now send it when they tag users, hosts, clients, groups and Entra ID objects.

The tag threat-count query for a tag now takes object names from all objects (display name, then unique name, then id), which fixes the wrong or missing computer name shown for tagged hosts in Top Threat Counts.

New endpoint GET api/v1/UserLocationCount/byUserId?userId=<guid> returns a data table of the locations a user signed in from. Each row has UserName, LocationId, LocationName, City, State, CountryOrRegion, FirstAccessTime, LastAccessTime, Count, UserLinkedId and UserDisplayName. It requires the User claim.
New endpoint GET api/v1/UserLocationCount?skip=&take= lists user location counts. skip and take below 0 return 400, and an empty result returns 404.

New endpoint GET api/v1/EvLocation/byIds?ids=1&ids=2 returns location records for the given ids. An empty result returns 404. A request for more than 1000 ids is logged as a warning but still answered.
Database view user_location_summary and a count column widened from int to long support the Activity by Location grid.

License upload (installing a license key) that Netwrix rejects now returns 400 with the LicenseInfo body and its ErrorMessage. Previously the failure came back as 200. A rejected activation is no longer cached as the installed license.

License activation error messages shown on the Licensing page: "The license key has expired. Contact Netwrix to get a new license key."; "The license key is invalid. Make sure you selected the correct license key file."; "The license could not be installed because the existing license file is corrupted. Contact Netwrix support for assistance."; "The license could not be installed. See the License Service log for details."; and "The license could not be installed. <detail>" for other errors.

A trial license key file is deleted only after the key activates successfully, so a failed activation no longer loses the trial key. Existing license information is no longer removed before the next activation.
Subscriptions that email recipients no longer carry a stale shared folder id. On upgrade, shared_folder_id is cleared on every subscription that has at least one recipient.

The expiration date and time of new application credentials and passwords in threat evidence now use the viewer's local time zone, and two evidence entries, Dangerous Expiry (key credentials) and Dangerous Password Expiry (password credentials), are defined for the app credential threat.
Date and time values in email and evidence templates are converted with the viewer's UTC offset (dateTimeOffset register) and keep that offset when formatted, with dates shown as MM/dd/yyyy.
The Send Email action no longer breaks a threat URL whose host starts with 'n' (for example https://netwrix...). Only a '/n' outside URLs becomes a line break.
Default PowerShell action script now lists Primary Event Originating Agent: $PrimaryEventOriginatingAgent after Primary Event Host.
The Flag as Confirmed Compromised action for an enterprise application now reads the service principal id and app id from AzureEventDetails.App, so it finds the application instead of skipping it.

Syslog events from Netwrix Access Management (NAM) can carry upn= and ntname= fields. The perpetrator name uses ntname, then upn, then username. Blank values are skipped, which stops wrong display names for accounts that are not synced.

A display name change on an already-linked Entra ID user, host or client now updates the display name stored on events. This fixes a wrong perpetrator name on Application Permission Change events. On upgrade, the next Entra ID replication sync is a full sync.

gMSA, dMSA and sMSA accounts are no longer classified as computers, because only the last objectClass value is compared with computer. They appear as service accounts with the correct tags. On upgrade, the next Active Directory sync is a full scan.
Full Active Directory scan is flagged by migration FullSyncToFixServiceAccountTags (ad.sync_config.perform_full_scan_next = true).
Investigation event tables no longer return 500 for Entra ID authentication events that have no target objects.

Custom threats roll up per alert query parameter set. Editing the filters of a custom threat starts a new rollup instead of continuing the earlier threat. On upgrade, the Custom rollup criterion is added to all investigation jobs.

Job service setting Job:AlertCatchUpLimitHours (default 6) sets how many hours a custom threat job can fall behind before Threat Manager skips the backlog of events as overflow. With Job:InsertOverflow true (default) it records the skipped range.

Custom threat polling is two-stage: stage 1 stores matching events in the new alert_query_event table, partitioned by day with the same retention as events. Stage 2 evaluates thresholds from that table.

First Time Location now ignores failed sign-ins. On upgrade, learned user locations older than event retention or without a successful sign-in are deleted, and the threat is suspended for 30 days (disabled_until) while locations are learned again.

Impossible Travel no longer offers the File Tag and Process exclusion attributes, because location data exists only for authentication events. On upgrade they are added to the job's disabled exclusion types.
Impossible Travel has a new setting 'Trigger on Non-Human Identities' (name trigger-on-non-human-identities) so sign-ins from applications and service principals can also trigger it.

New threat ids: FirstTimeLocation 74, AuthMethodsPolicyWeakening 75, SecurityPolicyWeakening 76. Exclusion types SecurityPolicyWeakeningPolicy (26), SecurityPolicyWeakeningTargetSetting (27) and OriginatingAgent (43) are new.

Entra ID risky object sync is split into three tasks, RiskyUsers, RiskyServicePrincipals and RiskyAgents, each with MinimumWaitTime 00:01:00, replacing the single RiskyObjects task in the Azure service config. Risky agents are read from the Graph beta endpoint.

A failed TLS connection to a remote service reports: "A secure (TLS) connection could not be established: <detail> The certificate presented by the remote host is probably not trusted by <machine>. Import it into the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store (Local Computer) there."
Creating or updating a Netwrix Threat Prevention configuration whose name already exists returns 409 "A configuration with this name already exists." Configuration names must be unique.

facts.statement: Setting the ADMIN password after a reset works for an ADMIN account created on 2.7 whose login record has no password. The setup wizard reports the account as not set up when it has no password, so the create-password screen appears again.
Changing the ADMIN password no longer returns 500 when the password history holds a malformed entry. The entry is skipped and an error is logged.
The web server sends Cache-Control: no-cache for HTML files, so browsers load the new index.html after an upgrade instead of a cached page that points to removed files.
Index idx_event_server_name_lower on lower(event_server.name) is added.
New table ntp_grpc_config holds NTP connection settings (name, service, host, port, credential profile, certificate, SPN).

facts.statement: The standalone Integration Service installer is not a separate executable. The main installer (NetwrixThreatManager.exe) can install the Integration Service alone, by selecting Remote Services Only on the Advanced Settings page.
The installer has an Advanced Settings page titled "What would you like to install?". It offers the radio buttons All Services and Remote Services Only.
With Remote Services Only selected, the page lists a check box for each remote-capable service: Action Service and Integration Service.
If Remote Services Only is selected and no service is checked, the page shows "Select at least one remote service to install." and the wizard cannot continue.

On the Welcome page, an Advanced Installation check box shows the Advanced Settings page on a first install. The check box is hidden when the machine is already locked to an install mode, or when the command line sets ProductInstallSettings_PreferFullInstall=True.
A Remote install always shows the Advanced Settings page, so the selected services are visible before installation.

The Advanced Settings page is skipped when you select Modify and the machine is locked to All Services. When the machine is locked to Remote Services Only, the page is shown with its controls disabled.
When the installer is locked, the Advanced Settings page shows "Install mode is locked. Fully uninstall and reinstall to alter this value."
After a successful first install, the install mode and service selection cannot be changed with Modify or an upgrade. Changing them requires a full uninstall and reinstall.
A full uninstall releases the lock, so a reinstall can choose services again. The previous install mode and service selection are pre-filled in the wizard.

If the command line passes ProductInstallSettings_InstallMode with a value that conflicts with the locked mode, the installer stops. It shows the dialog "Install Mode Conflict" with the message "This machine is already installed with Install Mode '<locked>', but the command line requested '<requested>'. Fully uninstall the existing product before changing install modes." A silent run only writes the message to the log and exits with code 1.
The command-line variable ProductInstallSettings_InstallMode accepts AllServices or Remote. Default AllServices. It is ignored once the machine is locked.
The command-line variable ProductInstallSettings_EnableAdvancedInstall accepts True or False. Default False. It shows the Advanced Settings page on a first install.

The command-line variable ProductInstallSettings_RemoteServicesSelected is a number that sums the service bits for a Remote install: Action Service 128 and Integration Service 256. For example, 384 installs both. Other bits are ignored. Default is empty.

The command-line variable ProductInstallSettings_PreferFullInstall=True forces an All Services install and hides the Advanced Settings page on a first install. If the machine is already locked to Remote, the run continues and shows the locked Advanced Settings page. Default False.
The SbSetup launcher starts the Threat Manager installers with ProductInstallSettings_PreferFullInstall=True, so SbSetup always installs every service.

The command-line variable WebServiceCertificate sets the HTTPS choice for a silent install. Empty leaves settings unchanged, Unsecured selects HTTP, and any other value is the thumbprint of a certificate in the Local Computer Personal store. Default is empty. On a fresh silent install with no value, the services use HTTP.
Silent installs accept InstallFolder (default [ProgramFiles64Folder]STEALTHbits\StealthDEFEND) and DataFolder (default [CommonAppDataFolder]STEALTHbits\StealthDEFEND) as Name=Value arguments.
Silent installs accept Host, Port, and Database as Name=Value arguments for the database connection. Host defaults to localhost.

Silent installs accept UpdateFirewallSettings=True to create inbound Windows Firewall rules. InstallADModules=False and InstallEntraModules=False skip the AD and Entra PowerShell module installs (relevant only when Action Service is installed).
The installer has a page titled "Securing Threat Manager" that sets whether the web console and services use HTTPS.
The Securing Threat Manager page offers three choices: Leave settings unchanged, Installed Certificate (recommended), and Unsecured.
Leave settings unchanged appears only when every service already has an appsettings.json file. When it is missing, Installed Certificate (recommended) is preselected.
Installed Certificate (recommended) shows a list of certificates from the Local Computer certificate store with a Refresh button. You must select a certificate before you can continue.

The certificate list ends with the entry <Generate a Self-Signed Certificate>. Selecting it prompts: Generate a self-signed certificate named "Netwrix Threat Manager Self-Signed For <computer name>" now and add it to the Local Computer certificate store?

The generated self-signed certificate uses the host name as its subject, is valid for 20 years, and is named "Netwrix Threat Manager Self-Signed For <computer name>". If generation fails, the installer shows "The self-signed certificate could not be generated: {0}".

Choosing Unsecured shows the warning: "Traffic to the web console and services will be sent over an unencrypted connection, including administrator credentials, and is vulnerable to man in the middle attacks (i.e interception, monitoring, alteration and substitution). Installing a certificate to secure these connections is strongly recommended."
The Securing Threat Manager page applies to the Web Service in every install mode, and to the Integration Service only in a Remote install.

On Install, the Securing Threat Manager page appears when a service has no appsettings.json yet, or when Advanced Installation is selected. On Modify it always appears. On Repair and Uninstall it does not appear.
If you select a certificate, the installer stops with "Failed to configure the web service certificate" when the thumbprint is not in the Local Computer Personal certificate store.

When HTTPS is selected, the Dashboard shortcuts and the post-install launch open https://<fully qualified host name>:<port>. The port is the WebService:Port value, 5000 by default. Otherwise they open http://localhost:8080.

After a Remote install, the Finish page lists each installed remote service under "Remote services require additional configuration.  Please complete the following:" with Service Name and Status columns.

Each remote service status shows Checking..., Configure Now, Configured, or Connection Broken. The status refreshes every 10 seconds. Configure Now and Connection Broken open that service's configuration window.

Selecting Exit or Reboot now while a remote service is not configured asks: "One or more remote services are not yet configured. Are you sure you want to exit?" The dialog is titled "Warning" and has OK and Cancel buttons.
The installer adds Start Menu shortcuts "Configure Action Service" and "Configure Integration Service". Each runs the service with --config-ui to connect it to Netwrix Threat Manager.

Action Service is now an optional feature of the main installer (service SBTSDACTION, display name "Netwrix Threat Manager Action Service"). The separate Netwrix Threat Manager Action Service installer is removed.
Installing or upgrading with the main installer removes a machine's old standalone Action Service installation, so no orphaned SBTSDACTION service remains.
The installer starts Action Service together with the other services at the end of install.
The Integration Service is installed as service SBTSDINT, display name "Netwrix Threat Manager Integration Service", set to start automatically.
The Move Database button on the Welcome page is hidden unless the installed services need the PostgreSQL database. For example, it is hidden for an Integration Service-only install.
The database pages and database steps are skipped when no installed service uses the database (Remote install of Action Service, Integration Service, or both).
The "Install AD PowerShell Modules" and "Install Entra PowerShell Modules" options appear on the firewall page only when Action Service is installed.
With "Create Inbound Windows Firewall Rules" selected, the installer opens TCP port 55558 for the Integration Service (rule "Threat Manager Integration Service").
Firewall rules are created only for the services you install. The Event Service rules open TCP 10001 and UDP 10000. The Web Service rule opens TCP 8080.
The Welcome page has an Export Signing Keys button, shown only when the product is installed and a JWT signing key exists. It has no silent equivalent.

The Export page ("Export") asks where to save the export file ("Save the export file as:", Browse...). The default is NTM-SigningKeys-<computer name>.exe on the desktop. The name must end with .exe and the folder must exist.

The Export page warns: "The export file and the one-time code are secrets. The code is shown once, after the file has been created. The file is not code signed, so Windows or security software may warn about it."

After export, the Finish page shows a one-time code with Copy code and Open folder buttons: "Save this code now. It is not stored anywhere and cannot be shown again. Send it to the person importing the keys over a different channel than the file."
The exported exe runs on another machine, asks for the one-time code, and writes the JWT signing key to that machine's registry. It requires Administrator rights and .NET Framework 4.7.2 or later.
The export tool is installed under <install folder>\Tools\RegistryValueTransfer\RegistryValueTransfer.exe. If it is missing the installer shows "The export tool was not found at '{0}'."

The installer stores the JWT signing key in the registry (HKLM\SOFTWARE\STEALTHbits Technologies\StealthDEFEND\Security, value JwtSigningKey), protected with DPAPI Local Machine. Only SYSTEM and Administrators can read it. Service accounts must be granted read access manually.

On upgrade from a version that used <DataFolder>\WebService\jwtsign.pfx, the installer reuses the pfx private key so issued tokens stay valid, then deletes the pfx. A fresh install generates a new 2048-bit RSA key. An existing registry key is never replaced.
The installer installs the Microsoft Visual C++ 2017-2026 x64 14.50 Redistributable as a prerequisite. It replaces the 2015-2019 14.24 package.

The Visual C++ redistributable runs with /norestart. If it needs a restart (exit code 3010), the restart is scheduled and the Finish page shows "To complete the installation, the computer must be rebooted." with a "Reboot now" button. The system no longer restarts without notice.
The installer requires the .NET Desktop Runtime 10.0.10 and ASP.NET Core Runtime 10.0.10 (x64) and installs them when missing.

The installer requires administrator rights ("You must be an administrator to run this installer."). Windows 7, 8, and 8.1 are not supported. It requires Server 2008 R2 SP1 or later, and .NET Framework 4.7.2.
The bundle runs only on 64-bit Windows (VersionNT64 6.1 or later).
The Welcome page buttons now have keyboard access keys: _Install, _Change, _Repair, Remo_ve, and _Move Database. The finish page buttons Exit and "Reboot now" are unchanged.

The Report Only installer is built from the same installer source. It is named "Netwrix Threat Manager Reporting" (NetwrixThreatManagerReporting.exe). It offers only Active Directory, Email, License, Web, and Integration services.
The Report Only installer runs the License Service with the -ro argument so it never activates or reports a license.
The Full and Report Only installers share one bundle UpgradeCode, so only one of them can be installed on a machine at a time.

The database port list in the installer offers "PostgreSQL 18 (5439)" and "PostgreSQL 14 (5435)". The SbSetup launcher offers the newest PostgreSQL installer and shows a PostgreSQL upgrade documentation link when an older PostgreSQL is installed.
The installer waits up to 2 minutes for each service to start or stop and logs progress every 5 seconds. This fixes an install that appeared to hang at the PostgreSQL start step.
Installer code moved into a shared InstallerBA.Framework project; the old Installer.CustomActions project and UpdateAppSettings.ps1 are removed.
Installer MSI uses feature selection (CoreFeature, DatabaseSchemaFeature, one feature per service); the Locked registry value is non-permanent.
Database schema patches sql13 v3.2.19 to v3.2.34 are added to the installer payload.
Build scripts build-installer.ps1 and build-installer-report-only.ps1 were reworked to build one edition at a time.

The Action Service and the Integration Service each have a configuration window titled "Netwrix Threat Manager Configuration". The window header reads "Netwrix Threat Manager Action Service Configuration" or "Netwrix Threat Manager Integration Service Configuration". It replaces the console prompts for registering a remote service.
The window opens when the service executable runs with the --config-ui switch. The Action Service also accepts -config-ui.
Helper text in the window reads "Connect this remote <service name> to an installation of Netwrix Threat Manager using administrator credentials."
The Host row has a scheme drop-down with the values https and http (https is first and selected by default), a host name box, and a port box.

The Host name box is pre-filled with the fully qualified name of the machine running the service. If the service was configured before, the window instead pre-fills the saved scheme, host, port, and the Ignore certificate errors setting.
The port box defaults to 8080 and accepts digits only.
The up and down port steps limit the port to the range 1 to 65535.
Pasting a full URL or host:port into the host name box fills the scheme, host, and port fields, and drops any path or query.
The window has the fields User Name and Password for a Threat Manager administrator account. The user name and password are not saved on the service.
The checkbox "Ignore certificate errors" shows only when the scheme is https. It is cleared by default.
The Test button checks the host, user name, and password. The Save button stays disabled until a test succeeds, and it is disabled again after any field changes.
Validation messages: "Threat Manager hostname is required." when the host is empty, and "User name and password are required." when either is empty.

Status line messages are "Connecting...", "Connection successful.", "Connection failed." (or the specific error), "Saving...", "Failed to save the configuration.", and "Restarting service...". The line is shortened to 70 characters, and clicking it opens a "Connection Status" dialog with the full text or error details.

If the service already has a working configuration, Save asks "This service already has a working configuration. Saving will overwrite it. Continue?" in a dialog titled "Overwrite Existing Configuration" with OK and Cancel.

After a successful save, a dialog says "<service name> configured and restarted successfully." when the installer started the window, or "<service name> configured successfully. Restart the service to apply the changes." otherwise.
If the service cannot restart after a save, the window shows "Failed to restart the service. Click Save to try again."

Choosing http shows a warning that the connection is not encrypted, that the administrator credentials can be intercepted, and that HTTPS should be configured on Threat Manager first. Selecting Ignore certificate errors shows a warning that the Threat Manager server identity is not verified and credentials could be stolen. The warnings do not block saving.

After a successful test, if the service serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate, the window shows a notice and a Download... button. The button saves the public certificate as a .cer file (default file name "<machine name> <service name> Certificate.cer") to import into the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store on the Threat Manager server.

Saving registers the service with Threat Manager: the Action Service creates an application token named "<machine name> Action Service", and the Integration Service registers its own address and token.
The Test button authenticates with the administrator credentials only; an incorrect password shows "Bad user name or password" for the Integration Service.
The console configuration (--config) now shows the same http and ignore-certificate-errors warnings. Command-line registration (-url, -username, -password) prints the warning and continues.

The console prompt "Ignore certificate errors (press enter to use false)" appears only for https URLs and asks "Proceed with ignoring certificate errors? (y/n)" when true. The default URL is https://<machine FQDN>:8080 and the default user name is admin.
A localhost or 127.0.0.1 host in the URL is replaced with the machine's fully qualified name so Threat Manager can reach it.
The service exits with 0 on success, 1 when the chosen operation did not complete (for example the window closed without saving), and 2 on an unexpected error.
The remote services use a shared configuration dialog class and a service-name check for restarts.

Running the service with --check-status runs without a window and exits 0 (configured and working), 1 (not configured), or 2 (configured but the connection fails). On failure it prints one line starting with "check-status-error: " followed by the reason.
The Action Service status check tests the saved token. Failure message: "The stored token was rejected or the server could not be reached."
Not-configured message: "This service has not been configured."

The Integration Service status check asks Threat Manager to call back to the service, so it passes only when the service reaches Threat Manager and Threat Manager reaches the service. Failure messages: "No service status token is stored. Register this service again.", "Threat Manager rejected the service status token. Register this service again.", "Threat Manager does not have this service registered (HTTP 404).", and "Could not reach Threat Manager at <url>: <reason>".

Threat Manager reports a failed call-back with "Threat Manager could not connect to the Integration Service at <url>: <reason>" or "Threat Manager has no address or token registered for the Integration Service on '<name>'."

TLS certificate failures show "A secure (TLS) connection could not be established: <detail> The certificate presented by the remote host is probably not trusted by <Threat Manager | this machine>. Import it into the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store (Local Computer) there."
A service registered before 3.4 has no status token, so its connection cannot be verified until it is registered again.
Registering an Integration Service now returns a status token that can only run the connection status check. The token is not stored by Threat Manager.

The Integration Service saves its Threat Manager URL, the Ignore certificate errors choice, and the encrypted status token in C:\ProgramData\STEALTHbits\StealthDEFEND\IntegrationService\appsettings.user.json. The Action Service saves its settings in the ActionService folder of the same parent folder.

The Integration Service listens on port 55558 by default ("urls": "http://*:55558" and WebService:Port 55558). When WebService:Certificate is set, it serves HTTPS on WebService:Port and registers an https address. Otherwise it registers an http address on the port in "urls".
The address registered for the Integration Service uses the first host in AllowedHosts, or the machine's fully qualified name when AllowedHosts is * or contains a wildcard.
The Integration Service has an authenticated test endpoint, api/v1/TestConnection/Authorized, that returns OK only for a valid token.
The Integration Service Originating Agent filter for event queries is supported.

Threat Manager relays Netwrix Threat Prevention (NTP) requests through a chosen Integration Service over gRPC: get license data, get Defend settings, set Defend settings, and fetch the NTP certificate. The Integration Service logs in to NTP with the profile credentials and the Kerberos SPN set on the NTP configuration.

facts.statement: Syslog input recognizes the new fields upn= and ntname=. The perpetrator name is taken from ntname first, then upn, then username, then usrname. An empty ntname or upn is skipped.
A storage account perpetrator with the reserved storage key GUID now always shows the reserved storage key name, instead of being prefixed with the domain.

The variable $PrimaryEventOriginatingAgent (description "The agent that originated the primary event.") is available in actions and SIEM templates. It shows "Primary Event Originating Agent Not Available" when empty.
The default PowerShell script text of the action templates now includes the line "Primary Event Originating Agent: $PrimaryEventOriginatingAgent" after the Primary Event Host line.
Investigation queries can filter on an Originating Agent attribute in the Event group. The filter is case-insensitive and uses the agent name.
The Send Email action keeps URLs intact when converting the /n line break to HTML, so $threaturl and other links no longer break when the Threat Manager host name starts with n.
Threat email summaries use the same URL-safe /n conversion.
A /n directly attached to a URL with no separator stays part of the URL.
Tag Object action: when the perpetrator, host, client, or affected objects are tagged, each tagged object now sends its unique name with its ID, and duplicate IDs are removed.
Flag Compromised User action for Entra ID reads the application and service principal IDs from the event details, so a service principal or application perpetrator is flagged.
Action messages say Netwrix Threat Manager instead of StealthDEFEND: "Failed to communicate with the Netwrix Threat Manager REST API."
Action service stored token and password parameters are now encrypted with the common data protection layer, in a form the remote Action Service can read.
On upgrade, email subscriptions that had a shared folder ID set by mistake have it cleared.

On the subscription page, a monthly subscription or export using a Netwrix Threat Prevention source shows "For a monthly subscription, make sure event retention in Netwrix Threat Prevention is set to at least one month." Other sources keep the Time to Retain Events message with a link to settings.

The Risky Objects sync is split into three syncs listed in sync history as "Risky Users", "Risky Service Principals", and "Risky Agents". Each has a minimum wait of 00:01:00 (one minute). "Risky Objects" remains only for older history rows.
Risky Agents are read from the Microsoft Graph beta endpoint because the risky agent endpoint has no v1.0 release.
A blueprint is tagged with the highest risk of its agent identities. Confirmed Compromised replaces At Risk tags, and a not-risky object has both tags removed.

Display names of already-linked Entra ID users, clients, and hosts in event data are updated when the object's display name changes in sync. The upgrade schedules a full replication sync to correct existing names.
The Entra ID service principal sync no longer overwrites the Agent Identity, Agent Blueprint Principal, and blueprint link values set by other syncs.
Marking service principals as agent identity or blueprint principal now updates the service principal rows even when the object rows already had the type.
gMSA, dMSA, and sMSA accounts are classified as User objects, not Computer objects, so they are tagged as service accounts. An object is a Computer only when its last object class is computer.
Upgrading triggers a full Active Directory scan so existing service account tags are corrected.

A background check marks application tokens as broken when they are expired or no longer signed with the current signing key (Integration and Agent tokens are skipped). Audit log entries read "App token '<name>' is no longer signed with the current signing key." and "App token '<name>' issue has been resolved."

The services sign login tokens with an RSA private key stored in the registry value JwtSigningKey under HKLM\SOFTWARE\STEALTHbits Technologies\StealthDEFEND\Security. The key is protected with DPAPI using the Local Machine scope.
The installer generates the JWT signing key on a fresh install. If a signing key already exists in the registry, the installer leaves it unchanged.

On upgrade, the installer reuses the private key from the old jwtsign.pfx (%ProgramData%\STEALTHbits\StealthDEFEND\WebService\jwtsign.pfx) so tokens already issued stay valid, then deletes the file. The customer does not re-enter the certificate password.

If the installer cannot read the old jwtsign.pfx (for example no appsettings.json references it, so its password is unknown), it logs a warning, leaves the file in place, and generates a new key. Tokens signed with the old key then stop validating.
The installer step is named "Configure JWT Signing Key" and fails with "Failed to configure the JWT signing key: {reason}" if it cannot store the key.

The Security registry key is readable only by SYSTEM and Administrators. A service that runs as another account needs read access granted manually. Otherwise it fails to start and logs: "Unable to load the JWT signing key from the registry: {reason} The service account needs read access to HKLM\SOFTWARE\STEALTHbits Technologies\StealthDEFEND\Security."

When the registry key does not exist, a service uses the certificate named by the Jwt:CertificateThumbprint setting, looked up in the LocalMachine\My store. If that certificate cannot be loaded, the service fails to start with "Unable to load the JWT certificate with thumbprint '{thumbprint}': {reason}".

The Jwt:CertificateFile, Jwt:CertificateEncryptedPassword, and Jwt:CertificatePassword settings are no longer read. A service that still has any of them and no registry signing key fails to start with "Legacy JWT signing key configured. Re-run the installer to update it". Re-run the installer to migrate.

With no registry key, no thumbprint, and no legacy settings, a service falls back to an insecure built-in symmetric key and prints "WARNING: Use of symmetric key is insecure. Re-run the installer to generate a secure JWT signing key".
The installer script installerFiles/scripts/UpdateAppSettings.ps1, which generated the JWT certificate and updated each service's appsettings, was removed from the product.

The installer's Welcome page has a Modify action named "Export Signing Keys" (button text "_Export Signing Keys"). It creates a single-file .exe that carries the signing key encrypted with a one-time code. It is interactive only and has no command-line variant.

The export page says: "Choose where to save the export file. A one-time code is generated when the file is created." and warns: "The export file and the one-time code are secrets. The code is shown once, after the file has been created. The file is not code signed, so Windows or security software may warn about it."
Export failure messages: "The export tool was not found at '{0}'." and "Exporting the signing keys failed: {0}".

To move the signing key to another host, run the exported .exe as an Administrator on the new host and enter the one-time code. The key is re-protected with that host's DPAPI and written to the registry with the same restricted access. Restart the services afterward.
The signing key is bound to the machine through DPAPI Local Machine, so copying the registry value to another host does not work.

Threat Manager checks application tokens at service start. A token is flagged broken when it has expired or is no longer signed with the current signing key (for example after the signing key changes). Integration and Agent tokens are skipped.
A banner at the top of the console reads "App tokens are no longer valid and must be refreshed. ({names})" and links to the App Tokens integration page. It lists up to three names, then "and N more".

Audit log entries record when an app token breaks and when it is resolved: "App token '{appToken}' is no longer signed with the current signing key." and "App token '{appToken}' issue has been resolved."
Viewing or copying an application token value is audited: "Application token '{name}' value viewed or copied."
The BrokenTokens endpoint (GET api/v1/Apptoken/BrokenTokens) returns the names of broken application tokens and requires the ShowConfiguration permission.

Encrypted values written to appsettings (service tokens, passwords) now go through an IDataProtectorFactory abstraction with three encryption levels (LocalHostOnly, HostTransferrable, RemoteCompatible). By default, HostTransferrable and RemoteCompatible still use the legacy static-key AES module, and LocalHostOnly uses DPAPI Current User. Optional Encryption:{level} settings can override the module.
Existing values encrypted with the old AES format still decrypt: a value that is not in the new token format is read as legacy.
The _FIPS_Compliant (or FIPS-Compliant) setting defaults to True.
A rejected license activation no longer shows "Installed license." on the Licensing page. The page keeps the current license and shows the error in red.
Uploading an expired license key shows "The license key has expired. Contact Netwrix to get a new license key."
Uploading an invalid key shows "The license key is invalid. Make sure you selected the correct license key file."
When activation fails with "License activation error 2", the page shows "The license could not be installed because the existing license file is corrupted. Contact Netwrix support for assistance."

Any other activation error shows "The license could not be installed. {original message}". If no message is available it shows "The license could not be installed. See the License Service log for details." The original message is written to the License Service log.

The License API now returns HTTP 400 with the license information when activation is rejected, and logs a warning "License activation rejected". Uploading requires the ShowConfiguration permission and is audited as LicenseUpdated.
A rejected activation is not cached, so reloading the page does not keep showing the error and the installed license is unchanged.
Installing a license key no longer removes existing license aliases before activation, so a failed or repeated activation no longer leaves license information removed.
The bundled trial key file ({ProductName}_Trial.key) is deleted only after it activates successfully. If activation fails, the file stays in place.
A ReportOnly install does not activate or consume the bundled trial key, so a later upgrade to Full still gets a trial period.

facts.statement: New role permission ViewAllInvestigations: shows every saved investigation regardless of owner, public flag, or explicit access grants. The upgrade grants it to the built-in Administrators and Report Administrator roles.
Report Administrator no longer sees all investigations through a role-name check. It sees them through the ViewAllInvestigations permission, which the upgrade grants to that role.

Built-in roles (Administrators, Report Administrator, Report Reviewer, Responders, Response Managers, Reviewers) are all marked built-in. Updating or deleting one fails with "Role '{name}' is built-in and cannot be updated." or "Role '{name}' is built-in and cannot be deleted."

Permission list in the Role API: FullControl (0), ShowConfiguration (1), ExecuteActions (2), AlterActions (3), AlterInvestigations (4), ShowAuditLogs (5), ShowSearch (6), ShowThreat (7), CreateThreat (8), ShowHome (9), ShowSubscription (10), ShowServiceAccounts (11), ManageNtp (12), ViewAllInvestigations (13). Roles now return a Permissions list instead of one boolean per permission.
FullControl bypasses every permission check and is assigned to the Administrators role.
A new Agent token type (AppTokenType Agent) is used by NTP/NAM agents to send event data. It grants no console or API access and cannot be assigned through role management.

Changing the ADMIN password on the login screen no longer returns a 500 error when the password history contains a malformed entry. The malformed entry is skipped and logged, and the change goes through.

An ADMIN account created on version 2.7 and later reset can now set a password and sign in. If the ADMIN record exists without a password, the setup check treats ADMIN as not set up and the login screen offers the create-password step again.
Setting the ADMIN password on an existing passwordless ADMIN record repairs its links to the user account and adds the password, instead of failing.
The error message on the login, MFA login, and MFA registration pages is now shown in red.

The installer's "Securing Threat Manager" page lets you choose "Leave settings unchanged", "Installed Certificate (recommended)", or "Unsecured". It sets WebService:Certificate (a LocalMachine\My thumbprint, empty for HTTP) for each service that supports HTTPS. HTTPS is enabled by default for remote Integration Service installs.

The page appears on Install when a service has no appsettings.json yet or advanced install is on, and always on Modify. "Leave settings unchanged" is the default when every appsettings.json exists; otherwise "Installed Certificate (recommended)" is the default.

The certificate list ends with "<Generate a Self-Signed Certificate>". Choosing it asks: "Generate a self-signed certificate named "{0}" now and add it to the Local Computer certificate store?" The name is "Netwrix Threat Manager Self-Signed For {computer name}". Failure shows "The self-signed certificate could not be generated: {0}".

Choosing "Unsecured" shows: "Traffic to the web console and services will be sent over an unencrypted connection, including administrator credentials, and is vulnerable to man in the middle attacks (i.e interception, monitoring, alteration and substitution). Installing a certificate to secure these connections is strongly recommended."
The Integration Service uses HTTPS on WebService:Port (default 55558) when WebService:Certificate is set. Otherwise it uses plain HTTP on the port in the urls setting (default 55558).

When a TLS connection to the remote host fails, the message reads: "A secure (TLS) connection could not be established: {detail} The certificate presented by the remote host is probably not trusted by {machine}. Import it into the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store (Local Computer) there."

Integration Service connection check messages: "No service status token is stored. Register this service again.", "Threat Manager rejected the service status token. Register this service again.", "Threat Manager does not have this service registered (HTTP 404).", "Could not reach Threat Manager at {url}: {reason}", "Threat Manager could not connect back to this service."
Netwrix Threat Manager 3.4 adds a threat named First Time Location. It is listed under the Azure threats in the threat configuration list.
First Time Location description: 'Detects when a user successfully signs in from a country or region they have never used before.'
The threat is enabled by default and has severity Low.
Threat title: 'First Time Location by {user} detected'.

Threat description text: '{user} signed in from {location} for the first time.' When one new location is found it names that location. When several are found it reads '{user} signed in from {N} new locations including {names} for the first time.'
Evidence entry titled 'First Time Location': '{user} signed in from {location or N new locations including names}, a location not previously seen for this user.'
Only successful sign-ins are used to learn a user's locations and to raise the threat. Failed sign-ins are ignored.
Failed sign-in locations learned earlier are removed on upgrade. Locations with no successful sign-in, and locations not used within the event retention period, are deleted.
After upgrade, First Time Location alerting is suspended for 30 days while locations are learned again from successful sign-ins only.
A user added to Threat Manager less than 30 days before the sign-in does not trigger First Time Location, because the learning period is 30 days.
First Time Location only applies to events that carry location data (Entra ID sign-ins).
Rollup is on by default with a 24-hour window (1440 minutes) and can be configured. New locations from further sign-ins in the window are merged into the same threat.

Exclusions available for First Time Location: Perpetrator, Target, Client, Perpetrator Tag, Target Tag, and Location (to exclude specific countries or cities). File, Process, File Tag, and Affected Object DN exclusions are disabled for this threat.
The threat details page shows a world map in the 'Threat Activity' panel instead of the attack path. The map plots the new locations and the user's known locations.
Map legend entries: 'New location' and 'Known location (7 days prior to detection)'. Clicking a legend entry hides or shows that category.
Known locations on the map are the user's other locations from the 7 days before detection. The list is captured when the threat is detected.
Map hover tooltips list each marker group under 'New location' and 'Known location' headings.
Map controls: a button toggling 'Group markers' / 'Separate markers' (nearby locations are grouped by default) and a zoom button toggling 'Zoom to locations' / 'Zoom out to world'.
Locations without map coordinates are not drawn on the map.
If location data cannot be loaded the map area shows the error 'Failed to load location data. Please try again.'
First Time Location is one of three sub-threats raised by the same user, client and host summary job, with First Time Client Use and First Time Host Access.
Threat ID 74; the location history is stored in a user_location_count table and the user_location_summary view.
Netwrix Threat Manager 3.4 adds a threat named Authentication Methods Policy Weakening. It is listed under the Azure threats.

Description: 'Detects an attacker weakening the tenant-wide Authentication Methods Policy by enabling a phishable method, disabling a phishing-resistant method, or broadening a method's assignment to all users', described as a quiet, high-leverage precursor to account takeover.
The threat is enabled by default with severity High. Threat title: 'Authentication methods policy weakened by {user} detected'.

The threat is raised from the Entra ID audit event 'Authentication Methods Policy Update' in three cases: a tracked weak method is changed to Enabled, a tracked strong method is changed to Disabled, or a tracked method's include targets gain the all_users group.
A target broadening is reported only when the previous include targets did not already contain all_users.

Setting 'Tracked Weak Methods' (multi-value list). Default: Sms, Voice. Enabling one of these methods raises the threat. Explanation: method ids whose transition to enabled is treated as a weak, phishable authentication method being enabled.

Setting 'Tracked Strong Methods' (multi-value list). Default: Fido2, MicrosoftAuthenticator. Disabling one of these methods raises the threat. Explanation: method ids whose transition to disabled is treated as a strong, phishing-resistant authentication method being disabled.
Method names use the Entra authentication method ids (for example Sms, Voice, Fido2, MicrosoftAuthenticator). Broadening to all users applies to any method in either list.
If both tracked lists are empty the threat cannot fire (the service logs a warning).
Threat description text: 'The authentication method {method} was enabled / disabled / broadened to all users.' With several changes it lists the first 3 and then 'and N more'.
Evidence entry titled 'Weakened Authentication Methods' lists up to 5 changes ('{method} was enabled', 'was disabled', or 'was broadened to all users') and then 'and N more'.
Rollup is on by default with a 24-hour window (1440 minutes). In a rollup, repeated changes to the same method and change type keep only the latest.

Exclusion fields for this threat: 'Authentication Method' and 'Change Type', plus the Perpetrator exclusion. File, Process, File Tag, and Affected Object DN exclusions are disabled. The Change Type values are WeakMethodEnabled, StrongMethodDisabled, and TargetBroadened.
The attack path shows the perpetrator followed by the affected method names (up to 3, then 'and N more').
The current configuration state of the policy is not shown as evidence in this release.
Netwrix Threat Manager 3.4 adds a threat named Security Policy Weakening. It is listed under the Azure threats.

Description: Entra ID tenant-wide guardrails (who may invite guests, whether users may consent to third-party apps, whether Security Defaults are on, whether users may register applications) protect all accounts at once; the threat fires when one is loosened, a stealthy precursor to illicit-consent phishing, unmanaged external access, MFA-free sign-in, or app-registration persistence.
The threat is enabled by default with severity High. Threat title: 'Security policy weakened by {user} detected'.
Four controls are monitored, shown as: Guest Invite Policy, User Consent for Apps, Security Defaults, App Creation.

Guest Invite Policy is reported when the guest invite restriction becomes less restrictive. The levels, from least to most restrictive, are 'Anyone in the organization', 'Members and admin roles', 'Admin roles only', 'No one'. Tightening the policy is not reported.

User Consent for Apps is reported when the setting moves to a less restrictive option. From most to least restrictive: 'Do not allow user consent', 'Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions', 'Let Microsoft manage your consent settings'.
A move to a custom (non-portal) user consent policy is reported as weakening when a self-service consent policy was added. A move to a portal option from a custom policy is not reported.
Security Defaults is reported only when it changes from enabled to disabled. Re-enabling it is not reported.
App Creation is reported when the tenant policy that lets users register applications changes from disabled to enabled.
Source audit events: 'Update authorization policy' and 'Update company settings' (category AuthorizationPolicy), and 'Update security defaults' (category Policy).

Threat description with one change: 'The {policy} tenant policy was loosened from '{old}' to '{new}'.' (values in single quotes since TMR-1539); Security Defaults reads 'was disabled' and App Creation reads 'was enabled'. With 2 or 3 changes it lists the policy names; with more it lists 3 and 'and N more'.

Evidence entry titled 'Weakened Security Policies' lists up to 5 changes, for example 'Guest invite policy weakened from 'X' to 'Y'', 'User consent for apps weakened from 'X' to 'Y'', 'Security defaults disabled', 'User app registration enabled', then 'and N more'.

Rollup is on by default with a 24-hour window (1440 minutes). When one control is weakened in several steps within the rollup, the threat shows one change from the original setting to the final setting.
Exclusion fields: 'Weakened Policy' and 'Target Setting', plus Perpetrator. Both offer a fixed autocomplete list. File, Process, File Tag, and Affected Object DN exclusions are disabled.
The 'Weakened Policy' autocomplete lists: Guest Invite Policy, User Consent for Apps, Security Defaults, App Creation.

The 'Target Setting' autocomplete is grouped by policy and lists the setting a policy was loosened to: Anyone in the organization, Members and admin roles, Admin roles only, the two lower user consent options, 'Disabled' (Security Defaults), 'Enabled' (App Creation). The most restrictive settings are not listed because they can never be a target.
The attack path shows the perpetrator, a 'Weakened' key, and the weakened policy names.
Threat ID 76; exclusion types 26 and 27; the 'Weakened Policy' values are GuestInvitePolicy, UserConsent, SecurityDefaults, AppCreation.
Impossible Travel now has the setting 'Trigger on Non-Human Identities'. Default: off (false).
Setting explanation: 'When enabled, sign-ins from applications and service principals are also evaluated for impossible travel. When disabled, only user sign-ins are evaluated.'
Behavior change: in 3.4 Impossible Travel evaluates only user sign-ins by default. Application and service principal sign-ins were evaluated before and are now skipped unless the setting is on.
With the setting on, a service principal sign-in is tracked by its service principal id (or app id).
The File Tag and Process exclusion attributes are removed from Impossible Travel because location data is only sent for authentication events, so they could never match.
The Impossible Travel map is redrawn to fit its panel without scrolling the evidence, shows route and marker tooltips, and has a zoom button toggling 'Zoom to route' / 'Zoom out to world'.

The 'AI Agent' tag and the 'AI Agent' filter on the threat list now apply when an AI agent is the perpetrator, the target, or one of the affected objects of a threat. Before 3.4 only the perpetrator was checked.
The threat list shows an 'AI Agent' label on threats where an AI agent is involved. AI agents are objects tagged as agent blueprint, agent user, or agent identity.

Investigations have a new filter attribute 'Originating Agent' in the 'Event' group. It matches the name of the Netwrix agent that sent the event; values are free text or suggestions from an object search.
The 'Originating Agent' filter label is used in saved investigations and custom threats.
The same 'Originating Agent' filter is applied in integration (SIEM) event queries, matching the event's originating server.
Action PowerShell scripts and email actions can use the variable $PrimaryEventOriginatingAgent, described as 'The agent that originated the primary event.'
The default PowerShell Script action template now includes the line 'Primary Event Originating Agent: $PrimaryEventOriginatingAgent' after 'Primary Event Host'.
Custom threats are evaluated incrementally. Each polling pass reads only events added since the previous pass, so thresholds with long time windows no longer rescan the whole window.
Job schedules are ignored for custom threats. Every enabled custom threat runs on every polling pass.
A new custom threat, or one whose filters were edited, starts from the current moment. It does not evaluate earlier events.
Threshold custom threats total the event count (an event can stand for several occurrences) and trigger when the total reaches or exceeds the threshold count.
Threshold grouped by perpetrator: one threat is created for each perpetrator whose total in the window reaches the threshold. Events with no perpetrator are ignored in this mode.
If a running custom threat falls more than 6 hours behind, the backlog is skipped and the skipped range is logged. Setting Job:AlertCatchUpLimitHours (default 6) controls the limit.
Polling settings in the JobService configuration: Job:AlertPeriodInSeconds default 60, Job:MaxConcurrentAlertQueries default 3, Job:AlertCatchUpLimitHours default 6, Job:InsertOverflow default true.
Matching events are kept in a daily-partitioned alert_query_event table aged out by event retention; each parameter set has a cursor in event_cursor.

Risky users, risky service principals, and risky agents are now synced by three separate Azure sync services, shown in sync history as 'Risky Users', 'Risky Service Principals', and 'Risky Agents'. The single 'Risky Objects' sync is retired and only appears in older history.
Each risky sync waits at least 1 minute between runs (MinimumWaitTime 00:01:00).

Risky agent data is read from the Microsoft Graph beta endpoint identityProtection/riskyAgents with the IdentityRiskyAgent.Read.All permission. Agents get the 'Confirmed Compromised' or 'At Risk' tag by severity; a blueprint takes the highest severity of its agent identities.
The old combined risky sync (AzureRiskyObjectSync) was split into AzureRiskyUserSync, AzureRiskyServicePrincipalSync, and AzureRiskyAgentSync.

The Activity Summary tab of an object's details page has a new section named "Activity by Location" (for objects that open on the user details page). It lists each location with the columns Location, First access, Last access, and Number of events, sorted by number of events, highest first.

The Activity by Location section has a "Show On Map" button in the table toolbar. It opens a full-screen dialog titled "Activity by Location" with a close button, and plots every listed location on a world map (all rows, not only the current page).
The Activity by Location section can be exported (the grid export file is named "Activity by Location").

The Activity by Location section is hidden when the object has no location data (for example an Active Directory-only user). If loading fails, it shows the error "Failed to load location data. Please try again."
Location data comes only from Azure (Entra ID) sign-ins, so the section only has rows for Entra ID objects.
On the Activity Summary tab the table previously titled "Activity by Host" is now titled "Activity by Target" (also the export file name).
The legacy Activity summary widget heading "Activity by Host" is also renamed "Activity by Target".
The Activity by Target table export file is named "Activity by Target".

For AI agent objects (Agent Blueprints, Agent Blueprint Principals, and Agent Identities) the Group Membership and Roles tabs are hidden, because these objects cannot be assigned to groups or roles. Agent Users keep both tabs.
In a Report Only deployment, the Group Membership tab is hidden for those AI agent objects too.
Tag assignment sends the object's unique name when a tag is added to an object (fixes tags not saving the unique name).
The Description field on the tag details page now wraps text (multiline, up to 3 rows) instead of a single clipped line.
When the tag object picker is truncated it still shows the notice "Filter the query further to view more specific results"; the object lists are now virtualized checkbox lists.
The custom time range you saved with an investigation is shown on the Timeframe button when you reopen the investigation.
Custom time ranges show AM or PM. The Timeframe button and the StartDate/EndDate attribute display now use the format "MMM dd, hh:mm a" (for example Jan 05, 09:30 PM).
The StartDate/EndDate query attribute display uses the same AM/PM format.
The query builder panel has a collapse chevron aligned to the right end of the header, next to the "Run Query" button.

New query attribute "Originating Agent" in the Event group of the investigation query builder. It is a multi-select with search (object search results with object-type icons), accepts typed custom values, shows up to 4 tags then "+N", and supports the default operators.
The attribute label shown in the UI for the originating agent field is "Originating Agent" (the Jira ticket calls it "Event Agent").

Threat exclusion (Create Threat / exclusion editor) filters gain two new types for Security Policy Weakening: a policy filter and a target setting filter, each a fixed list with the "is"/"is not" style exclusion operators.
The weakened policy filter offers these policies: Guest Invite Policy, User Consent for Apps, Security Defaults, App Creation.

The weakened target setting filter lists settings grouped by policy: Guest Invite Policy (Anyone in the organization; Members and admin roles; Admin roles only), User Consent for Apps (Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions; Let Microsoft manage your consent settings), Security Defaults (Disabled), App Creation (Enabled). The most restrictive setting of each policy is not listed because a change is only reported when a setting becomes less restrictive.

The investigation Run Query screen is read-only for users who lack the Show Search permission (previously for users with the ReportReviewer role). Investigation folder visibility and the empty state follow the same rule.
Events table: the "Rows per page" selector offers 5, 10, 50, 100, and 1000, and 1000 rows per page works again (it failed after the data grid migration). Paging is server-side.
Events table pager text reads "from-to of total" with a trailing + when more events exist than the count shown, next to the "Rows per page:" selector.
The empty Events table shows "Run a query to see results" before the first query in Investigations, and "No rows" otherwise. Threat details never shows the "Run a query" hint, only "No rows".
If expanding an event row fails to load details, an error notification shows the server message or "Failed to load event details." and the row collapses.

Threat details Event Details and Related Activity tabs show a loading spinner and a working "Cancel Request" link when you change Rows per page, page, or sort. Cancelling restores the previously shown events instead of leaving the table blank, and each tab loads independently.
The "Cancel Request" link label in the loading overlay.
The Top Perpetrators and Top Targets tables on a threat's Top Resources view are drawn as cards with a visible border and fill the available height.
Top Perpetrators and Top Targets cards are enabled in Investigation with showBorder and fullHeight.
Service Accounts page search matches the Display name as well as the NT account name, and a search with several words (separated by any whitespace) must match all words.
The quick-search words on the Service Accounts page are split on any whitespace, not only single spaces.

The Service Accounts Type column shows User, sMSA, gMSA, or dMSA. Managed service accounts (gMSA, dMSA, sMSA) are now recognized by their specific class and no longer classified as computers, so they are auto-tagged as Service Accounts (backend fix; a full sync migration ships with it).
Service Accounts grid columns: Display name, Domain, Type, Status, Vulnerable, Password Age (days), Tags, Auth Protocols, Encryption Types, SPNs, Targets, Clients, Created.

Monthly subscription or export warning depends on the investigation's data source. For a Threat Manager source it reads: "For a monthly subscription (or export), the Time to Retain Events must be set to at least one month. Go to settings" with a link to System Settings.

For a Netwrix Threat Prevention source the monthly warning reads: "For a monthly subscription (or export), make sure event retention in Netwrix Threat Prevention is set to at least one month." with no link.
Editing an email subscription no longer picks up a Shared Folder ID from a previously opened folder-export subscription. The subscription form resets to defaults when the dialog closes.
The Subscriptions grid uses server-style pagination with row count tied to loaded subscriptions; subscription form fields were migrated to MUI 7 slotProps.
A First Time Location threat details page shows a Threat Activity widget containing a world map of locations instead of an attack path.

First Time Location map shows pins for new locations and known locations, with a legend: "New location" and "Known location (7 days prior to detection)". Clicking a legend entry hides or shows that category.
Hovering a First Time Location pin shows a tooltip with "New location" and "Known location" sections listing the places at that point.
The location map has two icon buttons: one toggles marker grouping (tooltip "Separate markers" / "Group markers"), the other toggles zoom ("Zoom to locations" / "Zoom out to world").
If the locations for a First Time Location threat fail to load, the widget shows the error "Failed to load location data. Please try again."
Impossible Travel map now fits the Threat Activity widget so the page no longer scrolls for evidence, and the duplicated Evidence block was removed from the Impossible Travel view.

Impossible Travel routes are drawn as curved great-circle arcs with a numbered itinerary. A place visited more than once shares one pill-shaped marker labelled with every visit number. A pair travelled both ways shows one arc with an arrowhead at each end. Hovering a marker highlights every leg it touches.
The Impossible Travel map zooms to the region the route covers, with a button to switch between "Zoom to route" and "Zoom out to world".
A stray raw description fragment (text after a pseudo new line) is no longer shown under the threat title on threat details (seen on First Time Host Access for Azure Storage AD-integrated objects).
Threat descriptions render the product's "/n" pseudo new line as a line break without breaking URLs whose host starts with n (for example https://netwrix...).

The threat definitions list groups three new threat types (ids 74, 75, 76) under the Azure group, and threat evidence uses new icons for location, authentication method, and security policy threat activities.
Threat activity icons: Location, AuthenticationMethod, SecurityPolicy activity types map to a location-dot, unlock, and shield icons.
Azure sync history lists separate service types "Risky Users", "Risky Service Principals", and "Risky Agents"; the earlier "Risky Objects" label remains only for historical rows.

facts.statement: The App Token detail page now hides the token value: the field shows "[Hidden Value]" until you click "View Token" (the button then reads "Hide Token"). Copy still copies the real token and shows "App token copied to clipboard."

An app token that is no longer valid shows an error alert on its page. For a policy token: "This policy token is no longer valid. All referencing policies will need to be re-deployed. Referenced by policy/policies <links>.", or, if replaced: "This policy token is no longer valid, but it has been replaced with a new token. Re-deploy the affected policies so they use the new token. Once done, this token is safe to delete." Other tokens: "This app token is no longer valid. Please create a new token and update all usages."

A red banner at the top of every page tells users with the Show Configuration permission: "App tokens are no longer valid and must be refreshed. (<names>)". It lists up to three token names then "and N more", and links to the App Tokens integration page.
A token flagged as broken is marked in the integrations tree (the App Tokens node label changes for broken tokens, as it does for broken credentials).

Licensing page: when installing a license fails, the page shows the server's error message (or "Error installing license") and no longer shows "Installed license."; an expired key is no longer reported as installed.

After an upgrade, a browser tab built against the old version recovers automatically (it clears the cached session and reloads from the root, once per minute at most) instead of showing the error screen at login.
Login, MFA login, and MFA register pages show error messages in red again.

New Windows configuration dialog "Netwrix Threat Manager Configuration" (opened with --config-ui, or the "Configure Action Service" / "Configure Integration Service" start shortcut) connects a remote Action Service or Integration Service to Threat Manager. Header: "Netwrix Threat Manager <service> Configuration"; text: "Connect this remote <service> to an installation of Netwrix Threat Manager using administrator credentials."

Dialog fields: Host (with https/http selector, ://, and a port that defaults to 8080 with up/down buttons), User Name, Password, and an "Ignore certificate errors" check box. Buttons: Test and Save. Pasting a full URL or host:port into Host fills the scheme and port automatically.

Dialog validation and status messages: "Threat Manager hostname is required.", "User name and password are required.", "Connecting...", "Connection successful.", "Connection failed." (or the error), "Failed to save the configuration.", "Restarting service...", "Failed to restart the service. Click Save to try again."

Saving over a working configuration asks "This service already has a working configuration. Saving will overwrite it. Continue?" (title "Overwrite Existing Configuration"). Success reads "<service> configured and restarted successfully." or, when the service is not restarted by the dialog, "<service> configured successfully. Restart the service to apply the changes."

Choosing http shows a warning that credentials are sent unencrypted and to configure HTTPS first; checking "Ignore certificate errors" shows a warning that it disables verification of the server identity.

When the remote service uses a self-signed certificate, the dialog shows a notice and a "Download..." button that saves the public certificate as a .cer file. The admin must import it into the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store on the Threat Manager server.

The web UI moved to MUI 7 and the Netwrix theme: data grid (free edition), tree views, autocompletes, text fields, icons, the System Settings tree indentation and the Investigations tree/favorites styling were migrated with visual-only changes (Font Awesome SVG icons, new custom DateRangePicker replacing the MUI X Pro one, removal of old theme files).

System Settings tree items (Auditing, User Access, Licensing, System Jobs with Abnormal Time Evidence, Automated Account Detection, Database Maintenance, Report Maintenance, and About Threat Manager) are unchanged.
Object details pages: the table columns no longer collapse after switching tabs, because tab content mounts only when its tab is first shown.
